name: vendor-lock-in
intent: Records what Vendor Lock-In costs: the switching cost of replacing one supplier, product, platform or architecture has quietly become so high that the choice is no longer a decision — and the price is that pricing, capability, availability and roadmap are now set by someone else.
problem: Business rules, data formats, deployment configuration, identity and application logic are written directly against one supplier's APIs, with no seam of your own between your domain and their product, so leaving means rewriting rather than reconfiguring. It usually arrives incrementally: each individual use of a vendor-specific feature was reasonable.
context: Hohpe's analysis is the useful one because it dismantles the binary framing: lock-in is not a property a system either has or lacks, it is a strike price. He separates vendor lock-in (difficulty switching suppliers, including commercial terms such as long-term support agreements that bought a discount) from product lock-in (locked into a specific product's APIs, configurations and features — an open-source product such as Kubernetes does not remove this, and heavy customisation is itself a form of it), architecture lock-in (Kubernetes usage implies small containerised services, so moving to serverless is not a small change), platform lock-in (a cloud platform holding your accounts, access rights and security policy, plus proprietary application-level services), and mental lock-in, the subtlest and most dangerous, where a team's absorbed assumptions reject alternatives. The AWS guidance makes the commercial framing equally clear: lock-in is really about switching costs making a move prohibitively difficult or risky, not about being explicitly blocked.
benefits: Terms stay negotiable: an architecture that could absorb a price rise has a counterparty relationship rather than a dependency relationship.

Capability and availability risk are yours to manage rather than the supplier's to schedule. Roadmaps, end-of-life notices and regional outages become problems you chose rather than problems that happened.
The domain logic survives the platform. Rules expressed in your own vocabulary keep working when the storage engine, the queue or the model provider changes.
Legacy exit stops being a rewrite. A migration becomes a data movement and an adapter swap instead of a re-implementation under deadline.
Security and compliance posture is auditable on your terms, because the control points are yours and not a vendor's default configuration.
tradeoffs: Some lock-in is unavoidable and pretending otherwise is the more common error. Hohpe is explicit: you cannot not be locked into anything, and you may happily accept lock-in when it buys a unique feature — his model has an 'accepted lock-in' region, and using a service because the migration is unlikely to be needed is rational, not a failure.

Every abstraction layer has a cost. Hohpe's cost model lists complexity (JDBC, containers and common APIs each add a moving part, increasing the learning effort and the chance of systemic errors) and new lock-ins (avoiding CloudFormation by adopting Terraform or Pulumi replaces one vendor lock with another).
Attempts to avoid lock-in leak. The AWS document is blunt about it: an abstraction layer over a leaky API does not make the API not leaky, so a change in the vendor's primitive still propagates.

Portability cuts both ways. Multi-cloud portability in particular reduces capability and operational simplicity as it reduces switching cost, which is exactly the trade-off most cloud exits do not quantify.
The cheapest mitigations are unglamorous and get deprioritised: define resources as code, standardise deployment with containers, and document an exit path before it is needed.

Not every system is worth the insurance. For a small application, using native managed services and accepting lock-in is frequently the right call, and rewriting to stay portable can cost more than the exposure ever would.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the system while the smell is present. The striking result is that maintainability, security and scalability are not the axes that suffer day to day — the system runs fine, which is why the cost goes unnoticed. Coupling and extensibility are what collapse, and only at the moment of a price rise, an acquisition, an end-of-life notice or a regulatory change, when every change becomes a migration. Security sits mid rather than low because you can still audit the vendor's configuration; what you cannot do is choose the control model.

participants.responsibility: Owns the product, its roadmap, its pricing and its deprecation schedule, and benefits from the dependency.
participants.notes: Hohpe notes vendors generally, more or less visibly, benefit from lock-in, and that lock-in also arises unintentionally from incompatibility.

participants.responsibility: Holds business rules, data and configuration expressed in the supplier's vocabulary, with no seam of its own between the domain and the product.
participants.notes: It is not blocked from leaving; it is simply priced out of it.

participants.responsibility: The interface owned by the application that the supplier is adapted to, so that swapping the supplier changes an adapter rather than the domain.
participants.notes: Absent in the locked-in system, and the first thing an exit discovers is missing.

use_cases: Business rules expressed in a database's stored procedures and SQL dialect, so the Oracle-to-DB2 migration quoted by Hohpe costs an arm and a leg.
Application logic written against one cloud provider's identity, storage, queue and serverless APIs, with no facade per service — the configuration AWS recommends against to mitigate the risk.
A platform choice that determines service granularity: extensive Kubernetes use makes a move to serverless an architectural overhaul rather than a redeployment.
A proprietary file format from a dominant vendor that is announced as a standard — the technique the Linux Information Project names as a way lock-in is created deliberately.
An open-source product adopted for its ecosystem, which removes vendor lock-in but leaves product lock-in in its APIs, configurations, custom extensions and commercial support requirement.
Team-level mental lock-in: after years with one stack, alternatives are rejected on assumptions ('scale-out doesn't scale linearly') rather than on fit.
avoid_when: The capability is genuinely unique and the switch is very unlikely within the system's life — Hohpe's 'accepted lock-in' region; using a specialised service because a migration will probably never be needed is rational.
The application is small and its whole lifetime is shorter than a plausible migration. The insurance premium exceeds the exposure.
The regulatory or data-residency constraints make multi-provider operation impossible anyway, so the abstraction would be paid for and never used.
The cost of the abstraction layer would exceed the strike price it insures — a thin facade over a leaky API, plus a second team's learning curve, against a migration nobody plans.

The supplier is a commodity infrastructure provider with documented, tested export paths (containers, object storage in open formats, portable identity). Insuring against a risk that does not exist is waste.
pitfalls: Confusing vendor lock-in with product lock-in. Choosing an open-source product removes the commercial dependency and leaves the technical one, which is often the larger of the two.
Mistaking mental lock-in for a technical finding. Hohpe names it the most dangerous kind because it is invisible in the code and shows up as alternatives that are never evaluated.
Adding an abstraction layer over a leaky API. The layer adds a moving part and the vendor's primitive still propagates through it, so the switching cost is unchanged and the complexity is new.
Assuming multi-cloud portability is free. It reduces capability, operational simplicity and often reliability as it reduces switching cost.
Writing the back-out plan during the incident rather than beforehand. AWS's position is that a detailed back-out or reversibility plan must exist before you need it, itemised by switching cost.
Refactoring to portable idioms that nobody uses. Portability enforced by lint rules against idioms the team does not know produces worse code and no portability.

related_patterns_notes.adapter: An adapter is the seam itself: it is the structure whose presence converts a supplier change into a change in one class rather than across the application. Its absence is what makes lock-in expensive.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: An anti-corruption layer is the stronger form of the same move used when an external model is hostile to yours — it translates between vocabularies so the supplier's semantics do not enter the domain at all.
related_patterns_notes.published-language: A published language is the counterpart on your side: a documented, stable interface in your own vocabulary that the supplier's terms are translated into and that survives the supplier changing.
related_patterns_notes.facade: A facade over each supplier service is precisely the mitigation AWS recommends — building a facade for each CSP service so it can be swapped out as transparently as possible.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: An API or service gateway concentrates the supplier-facing edges in one place, which is where an anti-corruption layer or a facade can be introduced without touching every caller.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: A plugin or extension point is the general form of the seam: declaring an interface you own lets implementations change behind it without changing the callers.

anti_patterns: Business rules in stored procedures: the rules are portable in principle and immobile in practice, because they are written in one vendor's dialect and depend on its procedural extensions.
Vendor identity and authorisation woven through application logic, so the application's authorisation model is a translation of one supplier's permission system.
Proprietary serialisation formats and file formats at rest, which make even a read-only exit a conversion project.
Cloud-provider serverless primitives (functions, queues, IAM) used as the application's only execution model, so a move is a re-architecture rather than a redeployment.
Configuration expressed in one provider's proprietary language with no portable source of truth, so the infrastructure is described in a language only that vendor can execute.
Heavy customisation of an open-source product, which is Hohpe's point that open source does not remove lock-in: the customisations are what make the switch expensive.

Architecture lock-in mistaken for a deployment detail: an application whose services only make sense as containers cannot become functions without changing granularity, state externalisation and messaging.
Mental lock-in: the alternative was never evaluated because the incumbent's assumptions were the team's assumptions.
design_principles: Depend on abstractions you own: the domain should depend on your interface, and the supplier's interface should be an implementation detail behind it.
Program to an interface, not an implementation — with the important qualification that the interface must be yours, since adopting the supplier's interface is the definition of the lock.
Keep business logic out of infrastructure: rules that live in SQL, a workflow engine or a cloud function cannot be moved without rewriting them.
Design for transience: build and deploy so a component can be replaced without a coordinated rewrite of everything around it.
Keep the strike price visible: an option you cannot price is an option you will not take, so a back-out plan is part of the design, not a runbook.
best_practices: Classify the lock-in before fighting it — Hohpe's five kinds (vendor, product, architecture, platform, mental) need different responses, and 'we are not locked in' is almost never true of all five.
Put a seam at every supplier-facing edge: a facade per service, an adapter per API, a port in your own vocabulary that the adapter implements.
Define infrastructure as code with a portable source of truth and standard deployment artefacts, so the description of the system is yours rather than the vendor's.
Separate business logic from application logic and document the rules, so a migration is not also a reverse-engineering project — AWS's explicit recommendation.
Standardise on open interfaces for the crossing points: HTTP/JSON, OAuth for identity, object storage in open formats, containers for the artefact.
Quantify the strike price per dependency: which data, which rate limits, which proprietary features, and how much of the domain is expressed in each. Rank the seams by that number.
Write the back-out plan when you adopt, not when you leave, itemised by switching cost so the plan is real rather than aspirational.
Budget for acceptance: some dependencies should be consciously accepted with a documented rationale and an expiry review, rather than quietly tolerated.
Watch for mental lock-in explicitly: periodically evaluate an alternative for the highest-stakes dependency, because a decision never examined is a decision never made.
sources: Gregor Hohpe, 'Don't get locked up into avoiding lock-in', martinfowler.com (Architecture Journal) — the five kinds of lock-in (vendor, product, architecture, platform, mental), the options/strike-price model, the accepted-lock-in region, and the cost-of-avoiding model including complexity and new lock-ins.

Amazon Web Services, 'Unpicking Vendor Lock-in: a guide to understanding and mitigating switching costs when changing your Cloud Services Provider' — switching cost as the real phenomenon, the six lock-in considerations, facade-per-service, IaC and container guidance, and the back-out/reversibility plan requirement.
